I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: For a captivity trauma profile, the threat pattern is dominated by loud sounds/startle and false alarms, but 'checking if someone is following me' implies a stalking/pursuit-based danger context that is not supported by the listed triggers or memory items. With strong Threat → Triggers and Memory → Triggers links, the threat content should connect plausibly to the trigger set; here the pursuit-focused checking stands out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within the memory node, recurrent replay and uncontrolled intrusions fit the formulation and trauma type, but intense shame on recall introduces a self-evaluative appraisal theme that is otherwise absent. Given that Negative Appraisals is not represented and Threat → Negative Appraisals / Memory → Negative Appraisals are inactive, this item does not cohere well with the otherwise sensory-intrusive memory profile.

For captivity trauma, 'similar cars' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile unless transport vehicles were a clearly central part of the trauma. The other selected trigger items and all Threat/Memory items point to a general captivity-style pattern of somatic/tactile cueing, intrusive replay, terror on recall, and hypervigilance to sudden sounds. A car-specific visual trigger stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of this formulation and is the one item a clinician would most likely question.

vignette:
Michael, a 45-year-old journalist, returned from an assignment abroad two years ago, forever altered by the three weeks he spent in captivity. He had been captured while reporting on a conflict zone, held in a cramped, dark room. He still vividly remembered the rough burlap sack placed over his head, tightening around his neck, and the repeated physical shoves and prods from his captors. The acrid smell of cheap alcohol, often on their breath during interrogations, had become indelibly linked to terror.

Upon his return, Michael tried to resume his life with his wife, Sarah, but the world felt different. His memories of the frightening event were like a film that played over and over in his mind, often against his will. These memories forced their way into his mind when he did not want them to, bringing back the same terror he had felt at the time. He would find himself back in that room, the pressure on his neck, the intrusive touch, the suffocating smell, even when he was sitting safely at his kitchen table.

This constant replay of terror meant that even the slightest reminder could send him spiraling. A new ache in his neck, a familiar stiffness from long hours at his desk editing articles, would instantly trigger a full-blown memory replay, overwhelming him with the sensation of the burlap sack. Similarly, the innocent physical touch from Sarah, a comforting hand on his arm, now often triggered a surge of panic, his mind instantly recalling the rough hands of his captors. The smell of alcohol, even from a passerby on the street or a colleague after work, would instantly transport him back, his breath catching in his throat.

Michael found himself living in a state of perpetual readiness for danger. He was on high alert when he heard unexpected or loud sounds, his body tensing, his gaze darting around the newsroom or his home. This constant hypervigilance meant he was always scanning his environment, looking for threats that weren't there. He often reacted as if he were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong, mistaking a dropped pen for an explosion or a car backfiring for a gunshot. This heightened state of threat response, in turn, made his memory even more accessible and intrusive. When he was superalert and watchful, his mind seemed to be primed to recall the most dangerous moments of his captivity, making the "film" of his trauma even more prone to playing, intensifying the terror he felt.

His hypervigilance also intensified his reactions to potential triggers. Because he was always on guard, his senses were acutely tuned to anything that might signal danger. This meant that the subtle scent of alcohol from a colleague's breath in the office, or a casual touch from his wife, or even a sudden neck pain, were not just reminders but felt like immediate threats, triggering intense physiological and emotional responses. He began to avoid social gatherings where alcohol might be present, making excuses to Sarah, who grew increasingly concerned by his withdrawal and reluctance for physical intimacy. His work as a journalist, which once required him to be out in the field, became almost impossible. He struggled to focus, constantly distracted by perceived threats, and found himself declining assignments that required travel or interaction in unfamiliar settings, impacting his career trajectory.

The cumulative effect of these experiences had become unbearable. Michael's constant state of high alert, fueled by the relentless replay of his traumatic memories, left him exhausted and isolated. He knew he couldn't continue this way, living a life dictated by fear and avoidance. The terror on recall, the false alarms, and the ever-present triggers had created a suffocating cycle that felt inescapable. He sought help, hoping to finally break free from the invisible chains of his past, but deeply afraid that the terror was now an inextricable part of him.
